Getting Started with Agentic QE

Your practical guide to beginning the journey from classical to agentic quality engineering with 60 specialized agents, 69 QE skills, and 13 V3 domains at your disposal.

Before You Begin

Let me save you three months of pain: Don't start with the agents.

I know, I know. You're here for the AI stuff. But trust me—I tried jumping straight to agents. Twice. Both times ended with me apologizing to my team and rolling everything back.

Classical QE Foundation
CI/CD pipeline operational (deployment < 1 day)
Test automation (integration & e2e) > 40% coverage
Production monitoring active
Team owns quality (not just QA)
Feedback loops established
Team Readiness
At least 2 champions identified
Leadership support secured
Learning time allocated (4 hours/week minimum)
Failure tolerance agreed upon
Technical Foundation
Version control for all test code
Test data management strategy
Observability stack deployed (recommended)
API-first architecture (preferred, not required)

Missing some? Start there. Seriously. Agents amplify what exists—they don't fix what's broken.

Your First 30 Days
Week 1: Baseline and Learn
Days 1-3: Foundation
Morning:
Take the PACT assessment (honestly)
Document current pain points
Identify ONE problem to solve
Afternoon:
Set up measurement baseline
Define success metrics
Share plan with team
Days 4-5: Education
Focus: Education
Actions:
Read the Framework documentation
Watch 2-3 implementation talks
Join the Agentic QE community
Avoid:
Buying tools yet
Making big announcements
Promising specific outcomes
Week 2: First Agent Experiment
Required: Claude Code Installation

AQE agents execute through Claude Code - the AI-powered CLI and VS Code extension. You must install Claude Code before using Agentic QE.

Option 1:
Claude Code CLI
Download from claude.ai/code
Option 2:
VS Code Extension
Install from VS Code Marketplace
💡 Claude Code provides the execution environment where AQE agents run via the Task tool
Install Agentic QE Fleet
# Option 1: Global Installation (Recommended)
npm install -g agentic-qe
# Initialize with auto-configuration (detects your stack, configures MCP)
cd your-project && aqe init --auto
# Verify installation
aqe --version
# Option 2: Without Global Install (Use npx)
npx agentic-qe init --auto
# Or for standalone MCP server (non-Claude-Code clients)
npx agentic-qe mcp
System Requirements: Node.js 18+, npm 8+, Claude Code (installed above)
Note: aqe init automatically configures the MCP server in .mcp.json — Claude Code auto-starts it on connection.
Your First Agent: qe-test-architect

Always start with assistance, not automation

# Initialize AQE Fleet (if not done already)
aqe init --auto
# Generate tests for a component
aqe test generate src/components/Button.tsx
# Or use via Claude Code (MCP tools auto-available):
claude "Generate comprehensive tests for Button component"
Agent: qe-test-architect
Capabilities: AI-powered test creation with property-based testing
Scope: One feature, one developer
Duration: 1 week experiment
Configuration: Located in .claude/agents/qe-test-architect/
Fallback: Can disable instantly
📖 View full qe-test-architect agent details →

• Test generation time: 2-3 days → 4-6 hours (60% faster)
• Edge case coverage: 45% → 92% (47pp improvement)
• Test consistency: Standardized patterns across team
• Agent learning: 23% improvement over 3 months

Introduce: qe-flaky-hunter

Now that test generation is working, tackle flaky tests that plague CI/CD pipelines

# Spawn agent in the test-execution domain

# Or orchestrate via MCP / Claude Code:
aqe task submit test-execution

1. qe-test-architect creates new tests
2. qe-parallel-executor runs tests in parallel

4. Agents share results via event bus
5. qe-flaky-hunter auto-fixes detected issues

Context-Driven School of Testing

The philosophical foundation of adaptive quality practices

Holistic Testing Model

Lisa Crispin & Janet Gregory's whole-team approach to quality

Lisa and Janet's Holistic Testing approach inspired our Collaborative (C) principle. Their vision of quality as a shared team responsibility directly translates to our human-agent collaboration model.

"Quality is everyone's responsibility, built into every step."

Let me save you three months of pain: Don't start with the agents.

I know, I know. You're here for the AI stuff. But trust me—I tried jumping straight to agents. Twice. Both times ended with me apologizing to my team and rolling everything back.

# Or for standalone MCP server (non-Claude-Code clients)

"We need AI in our testing NOW!"

I hear this weekly. My response? "Show me your current testing first."

Because here's the truth: Agentic QE amplifies what exists. If you have chaos, you'll get faster chaos. If you have excellence, you'll get amplified excellence.

Orchestration Strategies

How to coordinate multiple agents without creating chaos

The Orchestration Challenge

Picture this: 5 talented musicians, each playing perfectly. But no conductor. That's not music—it's noise.

I learned this the hard way when my 5 specialized agents nearly brought down production. Each was doing its job perfectly. Together? They were fighting over resources, duplicating work, and creating more problems than they solved.

Orchestration isn't optional. It's the difference between an agent mob and an agent team.

Core Orchestration Patterns
Pattern 1: Sequential Pipeline
Assembly Line

When to Use: Clear process flow, dependent steps

class SequentialOrchestrator:
    """
    Like an assembly line - each agent does its part in order.
    Simple, predictable, debuggable.
    """
    
    def orchestrate(self, task):
        pipeline = [
            ('scout', self.discover_test_scenarios),
            ('validator', self.validate_scenarios),
            ('executor', self.run_tests),
            ('synthesizer', self.analyze_results),
            ('reporter', self.generate_report)
        ]
        
        context = {'task': task, 'results': {}}
        
        for agent_name, agent_function in pipeline:
            try:
                result = agent_function(context)
                context['results'][agent_name] = result
                
                if result.status == 'critical_failure':
                    return self.handle_pipeline_failure(context, agent_name)
                    
            except Exception as e:
                return self.handle_agent_error(agent_name, e, context)
        
        return context['results']
Pros
• Simple, predictable
• Easy to debug
• Clear dependencies
Cons
• Slow (no parallelism)
• Rigid workflow
• Single point of failure
Pattern 2: Parallel Burst
Sprint Start

When to Use: Independent tasks, speed matters

class ParallelOrchestrator:
    """
    Like a sprint start - everyone runs at once.
    Fast but needs careful coordination.
    """
    
    def orchestrate(self, tasks):
        from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
        
        results = {}
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as executor:
            # Launch all agents simultaneously
            future_to_agent = {
                executor.submit(agent.execute, task): agent 
                for agent, task in self.prepare_agent_tasks(tasks)
            }
            
            # Collect results as they complete
            for future in as_completed(future_to_agent):
                agent = future_to_agent[future]
                try:
                    result = future.result(timeout=30)
                    results[agent.name] = result
                except TimeoutError:
                    results[agent.name] = self.handle_timeout(agent)
                except Exception as e:
                    results[agent.name] = self.handle_error(agent, e)
        
        return self.merge_results(results)

Example: Our parallel burst pattern for API testing reduced a 5-minute test suite to 45 seconds by running 10 agents simultaneously on different endpoints.

Human-in-the-Loop Workflows

Because the best agentic systems augment humans, not replace them

The Trust Equation

Here's the uncomfortable truth: Your agents will be wrong. Sometimes catastrophically.

A payment validation agent once approved a $0.01 transaction for a $10,000 order. Technically, the payment went through. The agent was "correct." The business logic? Not so much.

That's why human-in-the-loop isn't a limitation—it's a feature.

The Spectrum of Human Involvement
Level 0: Full Manual
Human does everything
Level 1: Agent Suggests
Human decides and acts
Level 2: Agent Acts with Approval
Human approves, agent acts
Level 3: Agent Acts, Human Audits
Agent acts, human reviews
Level 4: Agent Acts, Alerts on Edge Cases
Human handles exceptions
Level 5: Full Autonomous
Human sets policy only

Most successful implementations operate at Level 2-4. Here's why and how.

Human-in-the-Loop Patterns
Pattern 1: The Approval Gate
Agent Proposes, Human Disposes

When to Use: High-risk actions, learning phase, compliance requirements

class ApprovalGateWorkflow:
    """
    Agent proposes, human disposes.
    Safe, controlled, builds trust gradually.
    """
    
    def agent_action_flow(self, agent, action):
        # Agent analyzes and prepares action
        proposal = agent.prepare_action(action)
        
        # Add context for human decision
        proposal_package = {
            'action': proposal,
            'confidence': agent.calculate_confidence(proposal),
            'impact': agent.assess_impact(proposal),
            'reasoning': agent.explain_reasoning(proposal),
            'alternatives': agent.suggest_alternatives(proposal),
            'risks': agent.identify_risks(proposal)
        }
        
        # Request human approval
        decision = self.wait_for_human(proposal_package)
        
        if decision.approved:
            result = agent.execute_action(proposal)
        
        # Learn from human decision
        agent.learn_from_decision(proposal, decision)

Example: Our deployment agent has 94% approval rate after 6 months. The 6% rejections? All would have caused issues. Human judgment still matters.

Pattern 3: The Shadow Mode
Learning Phase

When to Use: Building trust, training agents, validating changes

class ShadowModeWorkflow:
    """
    Agent shadows human decisions to learn.
    Safe way to validate agent readiness.
    """
    
    def shadow_operation(self):
        while self.in_shadow_mode():
            # Human makes decision
            human_decision = self.capture_human_decision()
            
            # Agent makes same decision independently
            agent_decision = self.agent.make_decision(
                same_context=human_decision.context
            )
            
            # Compare decisions
            agreement = self.compare_decisions(
                human_decision, agent_decision
            )
            
            # Learn from disagreements
            if not agreement.matches:
                self.agent.learn_from_disagreement(
                    human_decision, agent_decision
                )

Quality Assurance

When to Use: Continuous improvement, quality assurance

class ReviewLoopWorkflow:
    """
    Agent acts, human reviews sample.
    Balances speed with quality control.
    """
    
    def agent_action_with_review(self, action):
        # Agent executes action
        result = self.agent.execute(action)
        
        # Determine if review needed (e.g., 10% sample)
        if self.should_review(action, result):
            self.queue_for_review(action, result)
        
        return result

        # Daily/weekly review sessions
        for item in self.review_queue:
            review_result = self.human_review(item)
            
            if review_result.incorrect:
                # Train agent on mistake
                self.agent.learn_from_error(item, review_result)

Queen Coordinator Orchestration

Hierarchical coordination with intelligent task distribution and consensus

V3 Feature
The Queen Coordinator Pattern

The Queen Coordinator is a specialized agent that orchestrates the entire fleet. Unlike flat mesh topologies where agents coordinate peer-to-peer, the Queen provides:

Intelligent Dispatch

Routes tasks to optimal workers based on load, expertise, and availability

Consensus Management

Coordinates voting for critical decisions requiring agreement

Work Stealing

Automatically rebalances work from overloaded or stuck agents

Task Submission Patterns
Direct Assignment

Queen assigns task to specific worker

Use case: Known expertise match
aqe task submit test-generation --priority p0
Fleet Operation

Queen coordinates fleet-wide operation

Use case: Load balancing, flexible assignment
aqe fleet run coverage-analysis
Orchestrated Task

Multi-agent task via MCP orchestration

Use case: Large tasks requiring multiple agents
# Via MCP: task_orchestrate({ task: "Security audit" })
Work-Stealing Configuration

Work stealing allows idle agents to take tasks from overloaded agents, ensuring optimal utilization across the fleet.

Stealing Triggers
Stale threshold: Task untouched for N minutes
Load imbalance: Worker has 3x average load
Explicit mark: Worker marks task as stealable
Health check: Worker becomes unresponsive
Configuration
# .aqe/config.yaml
workStealing:
  enabled: true
  staleThresholdMinutes: 15
  loadImbalanceRatio: 3.0
  preferSameType: true  # Prefer matching agent types

  # Protect certain tasks from stealing
  protected:
    - security-audit
    - compliance-check
Claims System

The claims system tracks who is working on what, preventing duplicate work and enabling smooth handoffs.

Available
No one working on issue
Claimed
Agent actively working
Paused
Work temporarily stopped
Blocked
Waiting on external dependency
Stealable
Can be taken by another agent
Completed
Work finished successfully
Claims Management
# Submit a task (Queen assigns workers)
aqe task submit test-generation --priority p0
# List all tasks and their assignments
aqe task list
# Check task status
aqe task status <task-id>
# Cancel a stuck task
aqe task cancel <task-id>
Consensus Voting Workflows

For critical decisions, the Queen can initiate consensus voting among workers.

Voting Process
1. Queen Proposes
2. Workers Analyze
3. Cast Votes
4. Consensus/Fail
# Consensus is managed internally by the Queen Coordinator
# via the MCP protocol. Example via Claude Code:

# Submit a decision task that requires consensus
aqe task submit quality-assessment --priority p0

# Monitor fleet-wide task progress
aqe fleet status --verbose

# The Queen automatically coordinates voting among agents
# and reports the consensus result in the task status
Consensus Algorithms
simple-majority
>50% agreement
supermajority
>75% agreement
unanimous
100% agreement
weighted
Expertise-weighted votes
Use Consensus For
Architecture decisions
Security policy changes
Breaking API changes
Deployment go/no-go

# Example: Feature Development Workflow with Queen Coordination

# 1. Initialize the fleet
aqe fleet init --topology hierarchical --max-agents 8

# 2. Spawn agents across domains
aqe agent spawn test-generation
aqe agent spawn coverage-analysis
aqe agent spawn security-compliance

# 3. Submit a coordinated fleet operation
aqe fleet run quality-assessment

# Queen automatically:
# - Analyzes task complexity (Score: 75 -> Tier 3)
# - Breaks into subtasks (generate, analyze, review)
# - Assigns to available agents based on expertise
# - Monitors progress and rebalances if needed

# 4. Monitor progress
aqe fleet status --verbose

# Output:
# Fleet Status: healthy
# Active Agents: 3
# Tasks: 3 running, 0 pending
# +-----------+-------------------+--------+
# | Task      | Agent             | Status |

# | task-001  | test-generation   | active |

# 5. Check individual task status
aqe task list

# 6. View system health
aqe health --verbose

# 7. Once complete, check quality assessment
aqe quality --gate

# Quality gate passes -> ready for deployment

Learning & Self-Improvement

ReasoningBank integration, dream cycles, and pattern transfer

V3 Feature - SONA System
Self-Organizing Neural Architecture (SONA)

V3 agents don't just execute - they learn and improve. The SONA system enables continuous learning from task outcomes, building a ReasoningBank of patterns that improve over time.

85%+
Pattern Reuse Rate
23%
Performance Improvement (3 months)
150x

ReasoningBank Integration

ReasoningBank is a vector database optimized for storing and retrieving reasoning patterns. Agents store successful strategies and retrieve similar patterns for new tasks.

Storage Structure
// Pattern stored in ReasoningBank
{
  id: "pattern-uuid",
  embedding: [0.12, 0.45, ...],  // 384-dim
  metadata: {
    task_type: "test-generation",
    domain: "core",

    success_rate: 0.89,
    usage_count: 147
  },
  reasoning: {
    context: "React component with hooks",
    strategy: "Mock dependencies, test hooks lifecycle",
    outcome: "Generated 15 tests, 94% coverage"
  }
}
CLI Commands

aqe hooks learn --name "test-gen-pattern" --description "..."
# Search similar patterns
aqe hooks search --query "React hooks testing"
# View statistics
aqe learning stats --detailed
Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

SONA supports 4 RL algorithms, automatically selecting the best one based on task characteristics:

Q-Learning

Value-based learning for discrete action spaces

Use: Task routing decisions
Simple, proven
SARSA

On-policy learning with safer exploration

Use: Risk-sensitive operations
Conservative updates
Actor-Critic

Combines value and policy learning

Use: Complex multi-step tasks
Stable convergence
Decision Transformer

Sequence modeling for decision making

Use: Long-horizon planning
Context-aware
Trajectory Recording
# Trigger a dream cycle for pattern consolidation
aqe learning dream --cycles 3

# View learning dashboard with trends
aqe learning dashboard

# Consolidate patterns - promote successful ones
aqe learning consolidate --min-confidence 0.8

# Export learned patterns for sharing
aqe learning export --output patterns.json
Dream Cycle Scheduling

Like biological sleep consolidates memories, dream cycles consolidate learned patterns during idle periods. This prevents catastrophic forgetting and promotes pattern generalization.

1
Collect

Gather trajectories from recent tasks

Continuous
2
Replay

Revisit and analyze successful patterns

~5 min
3
Consolidate

EWC++ memory consolidation

~10 min

Prune

Remove low-value patterns

~2 min

Promote

~1 min
Schedule Configuration
# .aqe/config.yaml
learning:
  dreamCycle:
    enabled: true
    schedule: "0 2 * * *"  # Run at 2 AM daily
    minIdleMinutes: 30      # Or when idle for 30 min

    # EWC++ consolidation settings
    consolidation:
      importanceThreshold: 0.7
      retentionRate: 0.95
      maxPatterns: 10000
Pattern Promotion Workflow

Patterns progress through confidence levels before becoming globally available:

Local (0-0.5)
Tentative (0.5-0.7)
Confirmed (0.7-0.9)
Global (0.9+)
Promotion Criteria
Success rate > 80% over 10+ uses
Consistency across different contexts
No negative feedback from humans
Passes cross-validation on held-out tasks

# Consolidate and promote high-confidence patterns
aqe learning consolidate \
  --min-confidence 0.9 \
  --promote-to global

# Reset patterns that are underperforming
aqe learning reset \
  --scope patterns \
  --below-confidence 0.3
Cross-Project Transfer

Transfer learned patterns from one project to another, accelerating learning on new codebases:

Transfer Command
# Export patterns from a mature project
aqe learning export-full --output patterns-export.json

aqe learning import-merge --input patterns-export.json

# Output:
# Imported 147 patterns from export
# - test-generation: 89 patterns
# - security: 58 patterns
# Skipped 23 patterns below confidence threshold

Transfer from similar tech stacks
Start with high-confidence patterns only
Monitor pattern performance post-transfer
Allow adaptation period before evaluation
Avoid Transferring
Project-specific patterns (custom frameworks)
Low-confidence or experimental patterns
Patterns from very different domains
Outdated
